text.p: V Oxford. Aug. 18 1732.
Dear Brother,

I am ashamed that you have not heard from me since my flight to Oxford with Mr Atwell, but as I can make no tolerable excuse I shall say no more than to satisfy you that it was idleness and not forgetfulness. ... Mr Atwell and I were fit persons to be left housekeepers in your absence and then to run away from our charge: desertions of less importance have been punished with death. Mr Atwell believes you think him executed already by his not having heard from you, but won't take the pains any more to convince you of the contrary. I hope Lady Cowper has received benefit from the waters that the next time we meet our Laughters may be incessant, not being interrupted by any sickness except - you know. Pray my humble service to her with Mr Atwell's. To The Right Honble Earl Cowper
att Tunbridge Wells.
Exeter College. July 31 1738.

I should not have neglected to have returned an answer to your kind Letter by the same Post if it had come time enough, however I hope this will not come too late to convince you that I am very sensible of the obligation I lye under towards you for your good offices, and shall be very sorry when you will undertake the same
disagreeable Task on my Account, however I own (so good an opinion I have of your Master's sincerity) I shall now take the Gown with more satisfaction, indeed if you had not been so good to have taken that trouble I don't think I could with prudence have entered into the Profession.

The Conversation I had with Mrs Points was owing to one she had with you at Lady Sarah's the subject of which, such as it was, was myself. You agreed there that it was not feasible to get any place from the Court of any Value without having a Seat in Parliament which at the best would be very precarious and depend upon behaviour in the House, and that a patent Place for Life was impossible to have granted, and the former being upon behaviour might be taken from me at a Time of Life I c'd least spare it, and so leave me worse than it found me. I was thoroughly convinced of the Strength of these Arguments, and therefore said to Mrs Points I must take the Gown. Indeed I had Objections to it and have still, but what in time may wear off. The disrepute the profession is in at present, the fear of not being looked on in the same light by our own friends, which is the unavoidable Consequence of the former, the difficulty of behaving so as not to give offence to those of the same order who make it their business to scan every word and action, nay misrepresent both if they can have any prospect of jockying you out of your expected Preferment, these are all Objections, but the Principal remains behind. The great difficulty I shall have to bring myself to preach, indeed I think it is insurmountable. The Nonsense I hear weekly at St Mary's convinces me that Talent of talking sense is given but to very few, and I have not vanity enough to think I should be an exception where the exceptions are so few, and not Courage enough to undertake what I have so small a prospect of succeeding in. But there are Preferments that do not require it as Prebends and Canonrys which would be more suitable Preferment for me till I am better qualified or more used to the business of Preaching (if ever I do use myself to it) than any Parish Living. Being in your Neighbourhood would make me infinitely happy, but make me shut up my Lips for ever, for you are the last Person I cd expose myself before, but if you c'd content yourself with the saving
doctrine of such a one as Squires, and not insist on the venturing to hear worse, it would be the thing of all others I would choose, and whether Ldy Cowper or Lt Grantham succeed or no my Obligation to them is the same. I hope there is not the necessity for my being one of the Chaplains as you apprehend. My Lt James Beauclerk they have provided for without, and I shed be loath to turn Courtier when a Parson, who refused it as a Layman. I hope this one example will have some weight with my friends, but I hope to hear your further thoughts upon it . I am afraid I shall have tired you, and Little Caroline find more fault with her Uncle than her Pappa.
Heinz Hill. July 10 1739.

Mr Colleton has a Gardiner who is afflicted with a distemper which puzzles the most knowing Physicians and Surgeons to tell what it is. Some say it is a Calculous disorder which requires Oleaginous Medicines, each have hard words enough at command to show their Ignorance. The Fellow is a very fearful poor wretch, applies to every body, and holds to nobody long, that no day passes over without a fresh Doctor, for each of which he has a fresh Symptom, this not only puzzles them, but sets them by the Ears. Mr Colleton therefore desires that you would, if you can conveniently get him into Hide Park Infirmary, which by putting him into more able hands may be a means of reliving the poor fellow, and at the same time of restoring the peace of Reading.
L Bond Street. Feb. 13 1744.

You desired I with send you all the news I cd pick up. I can hear of none but what relates to the fleet which at present gives this disturbance, nor of that, any thing of certainty. The report yesterday morning was, that this fleet lay off at the Goodwin's, but in the evening, in Ormond Street, Mr Townshend, who was just come from the Chancellor's, said that it most certainly was all got into Dunkirk. This again at night was contradicted at St James's, and that only some few were gone into Dunkirk to take the Transports aboard, and that the main part of it still remained off the Goodwins, and this still remains uncontradicted, so the most likely to be true. A Messenger this Morning from Spithead gave notice that the whole Squadron under Norris's Command with be sailed by Six or Seven at furthest, so they expected news of it every hour. Orders are sent as far as Preston for the Regiments quartered there to be immediately on the March for Kent, although most likely they will come too late to be useful; the Militia in the Tower Hamlets are ordered out, and for the safety of the great cannon at Dover Castle, T. Hales was sent away immediately with orders not to stay any where 'till he came there. The Buoys in the Nor are all taken up, that the French may have some chance of being drove on the Sands. These are all the particulars I c'd pick up to day at Court and I have almost put them together in the same disjointed manner I heard them. I think all their precautions discover more fear, than is reasonable, unless they are mistrustful of People at home. If Norris's Squadron shed fail very possibly we shed soon see who and who are together, but 'till
then I fancy they will have too much wit to countenance an invasion, however they may wish it. I am going to St James's, where possibly I may learn more, which if I do, you shall have. Your Master this Morning I thought looked down, and very ill, which I was sorry to see. I hope it is nothing but fretting, and that he will recover his good looks with the first good news.

No further news to day, but that the Breast Squadron is certainly in Dunkirk. Mr Points says that it is without doubt that an invasion was intended, and that their orders were to land in the first place they c'd conveniently. This is denied by the Ministry at Versailles....
Moat. Dec. 8 1745.

I am sorry to find by your Letter that affairs are in so bad a situation, it is very different from what I cd have imagined with two such fine Armies it was possible to have happened, however I have still great Confidence in the Vigilance and activity of the Duke, and that he will be able yet by the interposition of his forces to save us all from this impending danger. If he once is able to bring them to a battle, I hardly am anxious of the event, and if that succeeds to my hopes, my fears of any Invasion will vanish. Indeed one at this time may be of fatal Consequence, yet I think it hardly practicable whilst our Coast is so well guarded, that on the whole though I think we are in a very precarious condition, yet I am far from looking on it as desperate. We have a good Fleet, three very fine armies, each one much superior to the Enemies, and the body of the People, excepting the Papists, on our sides, and ready as I hear in London to join the King's Standard whenever it shall be set up. These are all promising Circumstances, and such as must in human probability be more than a match for our Enemies, either at home or abroad, unless our day of retribution is come, when we are to be deprived of those blessings, we have either slighted or abused.

I think you are very much in the right of securing whatever is valuable in the best manner you can, and that it is the Duty now of every Nobleman and Man of Fortune to follow the Fortunes of the King, and to hazard every thing in the defense of his Country, but I still hope, that there will be no necessity for your undergoing the
Trial. Shed there be, and you are called upon to hazard your Life in its defense, you don't think I hope, that I can stay unconcerned here at Canterbury, and wait the Issue of the Event. In that case, wherever you are, I must be. I shall at least by it lose the misery of anxiety, and so serve myself, though I may be useless to the common cause. Could I be of real Service any where, I shd be glad, perhaps sometimes I might, if those who heard me were as much convinced of my sincerity as I am myself, but that is seldom the case. At this time however, good Service consists more in action than talk, and that I think we are not so famous for, though no good man wed shelter himself under a black Gown when it became an immediate Duty to lay it aside, which I take to be the case in times of very imminent danger, or at least to act so in it as to show he does not wear it as a Cloak to Cowardice, otherwise his exhortations to steadiness and Courage will only expose him. But I have rambled excessively from my first purpose, which was not to say what I could or ought to do for the Service of my Country, but what my own peace and contentment of mind wed oblige me to do in case that you were necessitated to put your resolutions in practise, and to beg in the mean time that you with not give way to any Melancholy Apprehensions which our present ill situation may suggest, but apply what I call my Sovereign Cordial in all difficulties and distresses, which (pardon the Preacher) is this reflection; "That every Man must be finely happy, if he has not by his folly and ill conduct forfeited all title to be so; or otherwise no one can be finely miserable, whilst it is consistent with infinite goodness to make him otherwise."
Excuse this scrap of my Pulpit Eloquence, and believe me.
Durham. Oct. 16 1746.

I began my last letter so late that I was obliged if I intended to send it by the post to make it a very short one. I have now time to make amends for it, if it is really a fault, though very little pretence from the little this place can send you worth your notice. I recd but two from Kensington, since your accident, so whatever number you favoured me above it, are lost to me. In regard to myself, I think my disorder is whimsical as you possibly can; but very vexatious at the same time, the shape it has lately appeared in, is an indigestion, which perpetually makes me, as Sancho says, eruct , this I can but attribute to the Spa water, which though good for my other complaints is allowed by my Dr to disagree and turn sour upon some stomachs, and what almost confirms me in this is, that 'till I began the Spa water I had no complaint in my stomach that I observed, and since then, never continued it for 3 days without having it to a great degree. Though I suspected this for some time I have often been willing to make further trials, as I found it benefit my head, and revive my spirits very much. Now I am resolved 'till my stomach has recovered its tone to discontinue it, and content myself with the Assa foetida and other nasty things the Dr has prescribed me. What
makes it more whimsical it comes without any warning. Yesterday morning I was in full health and spirits, eat my breakfast of chocolate and drank my Spa water after it, went out in the coach, the most summerlike warm morning I ever saw or felt this time of year, turning in at the College-Gate in our return a sudden jolt gave a turn to my stomach, brought on my indigestion and hysteric chillnesses which lost me my dinner, and hung upon me the whole day. Today I have omitted the Spa water and am much mended, took my airing in the coach as usual, and have since ate a good dinner, and with an appetite. You will pardon these little punctualities, the distance between us makes them satisfactory, and what you might judge me worse than I am, were I to omit. A little to explain my lunacy; it has been an observation of Dr. Askew's in all disorders of the body which proceed from a fullness of blood, the strongest symptoms always appear towards the changes of the moon, and this he says a practice of 30 or 40 years have confirmed to him, and the changes in great measure of my case occasioning that fullness upon the weakened vessels in my head, and consequently the occasion of the hysteric disorder being then more violent, for which reason he desires always abt that time, 'till I am perfectly recovered to live a little lower than at other times. I, from looking back to my worst bouts, find great reason to think him right in this particular, and so intend as much as possible to adhere in that regulation of diet at the time he proposes. I find myself rambling again backward to my own case, and wasting my time on paper as if I was writing to an Apothecary for advice. I will correct myself, and only add this one thing, that, thank God, since you are recovered the hurt you received, and are escaped so great a danger, I know of nothing that can give me an hour's uneasiness, but great reason in that and other things to be thankful and happy with my present lot. Was my health equal to my present ease of mind I should have no complaints to trouble my friends with. That, I think greatly on the mending hand, and hope soon to have "men's sana in corpora sano" ; which is all one can reasonably wish and more than, considering the danger I escaped, I had reason to expect or hope for.

I hope L. Car. is recovered of her cold and shall soon see it under
her own hand. A few weeks I take it will lodge her in Albemarle Street, in the meantime I think the less she sees of her poor Mama the better. I would give you, since she is so bad, the same advice, and approve much of your London scheme this winter. You will find it difficult and troublesome if the war continues to go abroad, and for my own sake I can hardly wish any obstacle to it removed. If I could hope this place could be made agreeable to you to spend your summer in, if you want to be at a distance from your misfortunes, it would make me very happy to attend you here; sometime of it I don't doubt but you will, and if all would be so to you, I am sure it would be to me. I should be much pleased was the issue of Lady Cathcart's quarrel with her Irishman to be the letting of that house for any term of years. I should be glad to leave Muffetts on so good an account, which to be sure has the misfortune of being too far distant from Colegreen, and though the situation of Jewin Water is not so good, yet the country makes amends sufficiently for that. I thank you for what you call your selfishness, and pursuing of selfinterest, which, though, as it sounds a little worldly, I must not indulge you in it, and therefore must desire you to give it its righter name, partiality to me, and then I shall not have so little of self love has not to set the value upon it it deserves. "Rust to a point and fix at last". Poor Win! I hope whatever change he makes in his life it will be for the better, and whoever he brings to Bedwell will make it still more agreeable to him. I thought that affair had been all over as lately I had not heard anything of it; but by his discourse with you, it is certainly concluded on; for being wearied with one kind of life is a proper prologue to the breaking one's intention of altering it, as it carries an apology (though a very unnecessary one) along with it. I am surprised that the Tar water should occasion a return of his asthma, as it is generally allowed, and he has experienced in other people to have been a sovereign remedy for it. If that medicine ever does good, it must have the same fair play all other medicines have of a regulated diet, and one conformable to it, otherwise the mischief it does is not fairly to be put to its account. As few who take it regard this, unless they are in very ill health I wonder it
has not done more mischief than it has: and think that people's taking it in so irregular a manner as most do with so little apparent prejudice is a good proof that it really has not that heating quality that is objected to it. Was not my nervous complaint to go off as I hope it will under my present regimen, I should be tempted to try its efficacy, as in most disorders of that sort it has succeeded, but I believe I shall find no occasion soon for it or any other medicine, so much I rely on the course I am now in.

Lady Sarah in her letters complained much of her rheumatism, but the wholesome air of Pall Mall has now removed all complaints, and she calls herself well. This Mrs. Cowper's attachment to London makes her believe, which I put her out of humour by laughing at. She, thank God, holds well, is gone to a Ball tonight after having entertained half a score city ladies at dinner. My residence, to my great joy, ends on Sunday, and afterwards I hope ('till the approaching Chapter) to have a few weeks quiet, which will go a good way towards making me better. My greatest plague is to find conversation every day for 2 or 3 visitors whose names I hardly know; but I grow more hardend to it than I used, as I now look upon it as a thing of course. Our joint loves to yourself and little ones. I should trespass the other way should I say more than that I am
My Dearest Br
Ire Aff, and most faithful Br and Served.
Sp. Cowper
Friday 17

I have, this afternoon, another obliging letter to thank you for. Pray tell friend Coote that Mrs. Cowper joins with me in congratulations upon his succeeding to a stall at Peterborough. We only regret, since he has set his face northward, he has not as good a call to Durham. Unless he is obliged to you for this preferment, I don't recollect on whose interest he can have had this little piece of good fortune. You have heard certainly of Mrs. Madan's fall down stairs. Surely we Cowpers are all in a tottering way. I am sorry she has not escaped so well as we!
Durham. Nov. 1 1747.

I flatter myself that my last found you safe and well at your Journey's end. I had the pleasure to hear you were so as far as Hains-Hill, and I hope the rest of your Journey was as successful. No doubt you found Bath in high spirits on our success at sea. All that wish well here were much so. The news of it came very opportunely to us, while Town and Country were assembled at the Deanery to drink the King's health. I feasted that day to the number of 66 or 67, besides serv'ts, and though at first the numbers a little discomposed me, I found myself at the end less fatigued than I could expect, which I attribute to riding out that morning. Our evening might have concluded with rejoicings in the Town, but our Mayor, being neither a Glazier nor a Tallow Chandler, he ordered a Bell to go round the Town to forbid Illuminations and Bonfires; so all the Loyalty was within doors, and at the Assembly Room, where there was a sumptuous Ball. The worthy Harry Vane, who came to my feast, was my guest that week for two or three days. They are now returned, and I have the pleasure of knowing my public life is over for this year, and that now I can enjoy my fireside in comfort, while I stay.

Lady Anne, I hear, has taken a house in Albemarle Street and will be there in a few days. What stay I shall make in Town this winter I must be obliged to you for a dwelling for, if it won't be
inconvenient for I shall grudge any new expenses 'till I have got clear of all my debts, which with good economy will be some time about .

You don't expect news from this corner of the World, and I hear none, that you cannot know sooner from other people. I have at last got Clavering's old Schoolmaster his wish, a Living in this County: that I hope will show Uncle I have not quite forgot him. It is at a place on the East Coast, called Shieles, and is worth ab't 90£ a year. The situation bad, amongst salt pans, and exposed to very cold breezes from the sea, but it is the very thing the old man pitched upon when it was before vacant, so I have no reason to think he will refuse it. I got the present Incumbent removed to another Living purely to make room for him.

Mrs. C. joins in Love to you, Our Compl'ts, to Cos. Spencer. I am glad to hear he is with you. I believe he wants repairs, and hope when the waters have put him into a good one, he will take better care both of his Mansion and its Inhabitant.

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Durham. Sept. 1 1748.

I came safe to this place, thank God, last Tuesday, after as pleasant a journey as heat and dust wed suffer, but as I travelled the common road met with no variety that can be entertaining. Yesterday I went to Newcastle and returned thence this Evening. My call there was to attend the meeting of the Sons of the Clergy, when there is a collection of the same nature, though very different value of that in London, and where my great presence was though necessary to give it some countenance. This was my first excursion to Newcastle and unless I have the same call, or some business, don't care whether it is my last; for so filthy, so dirty a disagreeable place I never saw. It has indeed the riches and trade of London in some degree, but with it the nastiness and filth of Edinburgh, the inhabitants of the poorer sort seem to vie with one another in dirt, and was Mr. Coulson ever inclined to entertain you with a beastly instance of it, he has one cut and dried which with match anyone of that sort you ever heard.

I believe it will make him value cleanliness as long as he lives, and look upon it as a invaluable blessing. I don't find in him any inclination for Scotland, though by his late ramble his friends at Hertford will think him ripe for any freak. I have great comfort in finding my house fit for ire Reception, the new part of it is as well aired as if it had been finished last year and the old so cleaned and smugged up by the diligence and care of Maud, that it is a wholesome at least though not a cheerful or elegant habitation. She is in high Spirits at having got the better of all the filth and dirt of the place, though the setting ab't it cost her some tears, I daresay of regret for the exchange she made for Colegreen.

I now grow impatient to see you, so I hope as Mr. Points is obliged to spend this Month in Town with his Master you will anticipate ire kind visit and partake of the sport of this Country sooner than you at first proposed.
Durham. Oct. 15 1749.
I hope I make up by the frequency of my Letters what they want in size and proportion, for I would not willingly fail in every Circumstance of a good Correspondent.

I am glad to hear that M'Uncle and Aunt are reconciled, I take it for granted, though you leave me to guess at that, that it has been
brought about by your good offices. I need not ask what share Madam Jane had in this reconciliation, but shoud be glad to know how she bears it, and whether she can look her sister in the face after her ill usage? for I think no assurance can go through so much.

Ire. two last accounts of Lady Anne gives us all great pleasure, and I am still in hopes that you may by degrees persuade her to alter her hours. Pray tell her we congratulate her upon her new purchase in Albemarle Street, I don't doubt her present amendment to be owing to it.

The accounts we have had lately from Midgham has undone all that Air and Exercise had been doing for the female side of my house, in short, Mrs. Cowper's spirits have suffered by them exceedingly, and Emily has been more like a Mope than a sensible creature for these last 3 days, but better news today has revived them, and I believe if Tuesday does not contradict todays favourable account of Mrs. Points they may soon return to their right reasons. They have kept in close quarters all the time, and poor Lady Caroline these last two days has been forced to head my Residence Table, which she very kindly undertook, and goes through as if she had been born and bred at the Deanery. To add to Ma'am Cowper's misfortunes she has had an exceeding bad Cough, which still hangs about her, but is not quite so troublesome. I have my Complaints too, but of a very late date, stooping down in the Library today before dinner I gave myself one of those wrenches in the back I complained of at Muffets some years ago, what is the strangest is, it was neither by a sudden twist or stooping low, but by a very gentle motion. At present it pains me a good deal, and almost makes me a cripple, but as I know a few days will set all right I am not uneasy at it.
I am sorry to hear that you have had a return of your Diabetes, I hope next summer you will pay another Journey to the Hot Well, and in the meantime use much of that water.
Durham. Aug. 30 1750.

This is for the same purpose as the former, to give you satisfaction as to ourselves, by letting you know our journey ended last Tuesday by a safe Arrival at Durham. Good weather and fine roads made the rest of our way as agreeable as possible: but at York we met with difficulties: it was the last Day of the Races, and every tolerable Room but one at the Inn was taken by the idle people there of all sorts. This with the dirtiness of the house, smell of charcoal, tobacco, and kitchen grease, almost put Lady Sarah besides her patience, or to use Lady Cowper's phrase, made her cloven , the worst was that Sunday intervening, we were obliged to spend near two days there, though the dispersing of the Company made the last more tolerable. The first news I heard there was that Chitty St. Quentin had been long ill of a Fever, and as yet not able to leave his room. I paid him a visit, found him pretty cheerful, but not yet quite recovered of his illness. He inquired much after you, expressed great Love and kindness for you, which, knowing you both, I dare say was sincere. I gave your Complts to him. I was not very sorry to have York prove so disagreeable as I thought it with turn out to the advantage of this place. In this I am not quite disappointed, for Ma'am Sall seems well enough satisfied with it. The Prison Gates
and the popt-out heads had, its true, some effect on the Lady, but I believe more by the Lively picture you drew of them one day at dinner. But in general both the Town and Country far exceeds her expectations.

I wait with some impatience for tomorrow, as I hope for a Letter from you. It is an intolerable thing that the Post must carry our Letters round by London. I believe it makes a difference of 3 days in the carriage, which fling us at a much greater distance than we really are, which God knows there is no occasion for. I shd have been more satisfied if we had left Lady Cowper perfectly well, but she seemed, though out of danger, far from it, when we parted, and I know the nature of that Complaint too well to be perfectly easy till it is wholly removed.

We are still without Bishop: the Conge` d'elire is not yet issued from the office, we shall be ready, when it does, like good subjects to elect his Majtys. choice: were we left to our own it with, I fear be a matter of greater difficulty. There with be at least 13 Candidates, and I shd put my negative on all but one . But, as it is to proceed in a less contentious way, and our only interest lies in unanimity, there will be no delay of our side, whenever our Powers come. Next week is talked of for it. I have had a letter from Butler: he speaks doubtfuly of the time, but believes it won't be later. The Bp of Gloucester, it is thought, will be his Proxy at the inthronization. Our Choir looks dismal, surrounded with Black Cloth and Scutcheons, but as it is the only sign of Sorrow in the place it is more bearable.
Dr. Mangy is in perfect good health.
Durham. Aug. 23 1751.

I am this moment almost come to this place, too late and too much tired to say much, and very willing however to give you the satisfaction I know it will, of hearing that Mrs Cowper, myself etc, are
well and safe at the journey's end. I was in hopes to have found a Letter here from you to tell me you are safe and well arrived from Bristol. The weather at present promises to be so good that I hardly doubt of your undertaking your Norfolk expedition, if you do, I hope it will be a pleasant one, and conduce to my Lady's and all your health.

Spen. Madden won't let me finish this Letter without joining his Complts to Mrs Cowper's Love and mine to you and yrs. He at present is wild about the beauties of this place, I intend to lower his imaginations tomorrow, by sending him into the Town in high Market to regale himself with what is filthy and nasty, for I believe at present he wed be as immovable from it, as Old St Cuthbert's body was formerly.
Durham. Sept. 24 1752.

Many thanks to you for ire kind Letter. I am glad to find by it that you are well, and have some hopes, as Lady Cowper has not yet miscarried, that though she is the Opprobrium of the Physicians she will now go on her time safely, and at the end bring you a little William that you may have your Bow well secured by its double string. I find by a Letter from Newland Hall that Will. Cowper's wife has a Daughter, it will be no advantage to them to increase their stock, but I wish yrs was, for though I cannot possibly live to see it, I should regret dying with the certainty of the Estate's going into that family. As for what becomes of the Deanery at that time, whether Chapman or Orator Henly has it, it concerns me very little. The Ministers may dispose of that as they think fit, the only spite I shall exert towards them on this occasion will be to keep it from their disposal as long as I possibly can.

I am just returned from our Abbey, where the Old Baronet gave us a funeral oration on our late good Friend, not quite in the Henlyan stile, but as agreeable full as if it was. It was a very short, but very affecting sermon, so much so that short as it was I thought I must have gone out before it was over. The Text "he being dead, yet speaks". I had an intention somewhat of the same kind, not knowing his, or suspecting he would venture on preaching at all, but I am glad for many reasons he undertook it. I doubt whether since even hearing affected me so much I could have decently delivered any thing on this subject, and I have not the vanity to suppose that the audience are not bettered by the Exchange. I have often wished Henly's Bones broke for his Impudence, but never so much as now. The worthy E.P.R. who is supposed to give this Lampoon, is one Edwd. Pickering Rich once Curate at Cheltenham-Wells, whom the Bishop silenced and turned out of his Curacy
for Preaching Treason, or rather praying Treason, for he had learned from his associate Henly to turn his prayer into sin, by making it an Abusive Libel against the King and Royal Family. What the scoundrel means by the Bp's not being reconciled to him on his death bed I can't conceive. I do not suppose that the approach of death would make him in love with blasphemy or Treason, or at all more engage him to them who were Professors in it. I have the charity to hope and believe, that even these two Wretches will look upon either in another light when they come to die, and be as little at peace or in reconcilement with themselves for the impious use they have made of their Function, as the Bishop could possibly have been in the height of his Resentment. I should be glad to know however the meaning of the last lines of the libel
...who shed a Tear?
Why B for Interest, and St P. for fear! for here he is so dark that his scurrility has quite lost its weight, by being unintelligible.
Your account of poor Lt Fordwiche's mistake has made us laugh heartily; he will look extremely silly when he sees my Lady next, or his Uncle Elliot, whom, I suppose, received the other Letter.

If poor Diamond should not get a Master I don't know what must be his fate. I am loath to pronounce sentence upon him, as I think he is not yet uncomfortable to himself. I have very little reason for my own sake to care about my wall-fruit, but am sorry for my Lady's and ire own, that it don't turn out well. There is something I hope to be allowed for the wetness of the year, which as affected all the Fruit.
I'll remember you to Mr Little.

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Durham. Aug. 31 1753

You will expect to hear I have finished my journey. It was ended thank God, last Wednesday, and with as little uneasiness to a sore part as I could expect. We took Sr W. Milners in our way, and rested there four days, this was a great ease to me, though one day there I was alarmed with a slight return, but living low and cool carried it off. The day I came here, our good Bishop retired to Auckland, and intends to stay there 3 or 4 weeks, so I have not yet seen him. He left however a very obliging Message behind with Dr Bland, which in some measure has relieved a suspicion his sudden retreat had raised in me, that the same college was not to hold us both. I intend next Monday to follow him to Aukland and see there whether it is practicable or not to be on good Terms with him; for I reckon my reception there will determine it. One bad symptom I think is, his strict Connexion with Lt Bernard, whom I hear directs him in all things, and with whom I am in disgrace for detecting his insincerity in relation to Ashley. This good Peer rages against the Memory of poor Bishop Butler, and t'other day in a public Company called him an Old Rogue and Hypocrite. Hypocrisy I think is one Vice his L'p is not so accountable for as many others, so he was in the right to make that the subject of his invective, though few will think that the Bp is hurt in the charge, but enough of these.

Our poor friend, Sr John is revived miraculously, and I think, if he continues to gather strength as he has done for this last fortnight, may bid fair for weath'ring the Winter. His Neighbour, Dr Leslie grows more illustrious, he is setting out for Ireland; but by his Conversation one would imagine he was just returned from it.
He has lately purchased two Coach-horses which completes his set, and somebody asking him whether he would not appear on the Raceground with his six horses, he made answer: "No my Dear now! not till I get to my own Country of Ireland: for was I to drive six here they would call me proud Scot !" This and his tying up his Weather Cock to the East to secure a fair wind are our great topics at present of mirth. Another piece of drollery has happened which will serve to fill up my Paper. Our Bishop the other day received an anonymous letter full of bitter complaints against a Clergyman of this Diocese; charging him with many immoralities, false doctrine, and corrupting and altering the Liturgy, besides the reading it in an irreverent manner: one instance of which was that in the Litany instead of "all Bishops , Priests and Deacons" he read "all vicious Priests and Deacons".

I have just had ire very kind Letter. Mr Crow who came in this Evening, desires with Compl'ts that I would tell you he thinks it Best for the Dogs themselves, as well as to avoid the hazard of Carriers, that they should stay 'till I return, when he answers for putting them into ire hands as staunch Dogs as ever was broke.
Durham. Sept. 1 1754.
My promising to write today is my only inducement as I have nothing to add to my last, but particulars of my journey from Norwich to this place.

I left the good Bp's Palace the Friday after I wrote from thence and with no small reluctance. To make the Pill go down the better he went with us that day to Mrs Townshend's of Hunningham. Its a pretty place altogether, its situation something like Lady Cathcart's as well as the House. The Grounds about it very Park-like and pleasant, but they are surrounded almost by a barren Heath and the Sands very deep. From hence I went on the Monday to dine with Horace Walpole at Wolterton. The House, which he built, is an extraordinary good one, very elegantly finished and furnished, and
particularly as to Tapestry, which is the best I ever saw. His Plantations are very fine, in the midst of which, opposite to his House lies a handsome piece of Water, inferior, but very much resembling Lt Cornwallis's at Culford. I found the Old Gentleman in perfect good health, and so stout upon his Legs (I wish you were so) that he ran with me into every creek and cranny of his House above and below, and afterwards walked me over all his Grounds and Plantations near home. He was very kind and civil, but I cannot say so much of Madam my Aunt, who entertained us with scolding her Servants all the while we were there. The next day we took our leave of Mrs T. and spent it at Rainham. Lt T. very grumpy to Mrs Cowper, but very complaisant and flattering to me. The House is one of the most comfortable houses to live in I ever saw, and yet it is full stately enough even for a Townshend . The furnishing, which was done by the late Lord, who refitted it entirely, is in a better taste than that of Houghton as it is not so tawdry, and the furniture he put in is very handsome, the rest being I believe the same age with the House, which I take to be one of the first of Inigo Jones's works in England. But the Beauty of the place lies, or rather did lie , out of doors, for this good Lt has managed matters so as nearly to destroy all that it excelled other places in. For he has felled the finest Trees in the great wood near the House, by which means the rest are so injured that they wont long survive the loss of their Brethren, and the lake is so neglected that it begins rather to have the appearance of a Marsh overflowed than what it is, and this only to save the expense of keeping up its head, which would not have stood him in ten pound a year. Poor Mrs C. was sadly mortified to see her favourite Spot, which used to be her boast, so sadly changed since she lived there with her Father, but she had the prudence to stifle it 'till she had turned her back upon it. It certainly is in sad ruin, but yet it has enough beauty left to be thought the finest place in Norfolk, I mean by those who prefer natural beauties to the modern artificial ones of Pagodas and Chinese Baby Houses. His good L'p took us out in the Evening to show me, as he called it, the Place , but it ended in the sight of two or three filly-foles at the bottom of the Park: and when on his ordering the Chaise to turn about, as I promised myself to view something
that was extraordinarily worth taking notice of, it was to show us a large Dunghill , which he assured me was of his own making, and the best improvement there.

Enough of him and his ill humours. We staid only that Night, and the next Morning went with Mrs. Townshend whom we again picked up on the road to Holkham. The Body of the house is coverd in, but I saw no part of it finished but the Statue Gallery, and Eating Room, which are fine Rooms and proportionable to the greatness of the Plan, the Egyptian-Hall is as yet an empty shell so I can say nothing of it. The Plantations are rather grown, but I fear it can never be hoped they will be considerable. The Sea Breeze is so strong, that not only the Trees but the walls of the house seem corroded with its salts.

From hence the day following I kept on my Journey towards the Fens by Swaffham and Downham, and saw Houghton in the way. The Collecting all the best pieces into the Gallery has a fine effect, though it makes the rest of the house less worth seeing, both they and the furniture are well preserved, but the outside of the house and about it betrays the want of an inhabitant.
My Paper is so near an end that did my remaining Journal afford anything more worth writing I shd not have room.
Durham. Oct. 2 1756.
I am sorry to find ire Letter of the 26th in my Pocket unanswered, but Residence must excuse all.
Things go on here at their old Rate. Mrs C. sometimes well, sometimes ill, and ire humble Served at this time neither well or ill.

We have had a most dreadful Hurricane here, exceeding that you may remember some years ago at this place many degrees. It happened on Wednesday night last about 3 o'Clock. I have only lost a
chimney, but the B'ps damages won't be made good for two hundred pound. The worst to me is, that it has torn all the Wood on the Banks of the River to pieces, and left that pretty place quite desolate. It looks as if an high-land Army had passed through, and done all the mischief they could. I hope you have escaped in Hertfordshire. I dread much the consequence, as to our Shipping, particularly Boscawen's Squadron off Breast.

I don't know how to flatter myself that ire Letter will succeed, if you don't, thank God it is not a favr you stand in any need of. I am more troubled about the ill success Heavisides has had in removing ire Palpitation. I cannot but think it to be Nervous and that Valerian and those kind of things together with Exercise will carry it off, was it any serious complaint you with not have intermissions, so don't alarm yrself about it, for that will only serve to increase the Malady.
As to Brown's sauciness, I believe you have nothing to combat it with but Patience. These are Hamlet's days, when the "Foot of Peasant comes so near the heel of the Courtier that he galls his Kibe."

Lt Darlington, for what end I don't understand, has all at once taken it into his head to return to his former Civility to me. He has been here twice within this Week, and promises another in his own Person or Lady's next Saturday. Are not we very happy? The horrid stories that go about of his Daughter &c lessens much I think the reputation of this Lordly Intimacy, and makes me very shy of encouraging it, and wish he would select any other of my Brethren to bestow the honour upon. Yet I don't know well how to avoid it here, except I do as you recommend for L'Hirondell, give him one of Johnny Keel's broad hints, and as he is our Lt Lieutenant I don't know how becoming that may be.

Talking of L'Hirondell, I had a Letter from him in Hertfordshire, but I left it unanswered as I shall all he writes to me, and I think you would do right to take the same resolution. There is no end of him. My Brethren are as tired of him, and with as much reason as myself, particularly Dr Bland, whom, knowing our Intimacy, he plagues Post after Post, so on the whole I fancy he can promise himself no good from us.
Durham. Sept. 11 1757.

The Sequel of my unfinished Letter, though not much to the purpose, shall now follow, and I recollect all my anecdotes of Raby were not quite exhausted. Our Lt Lieutnt chooses, as every one observes, to
sleep in a whole skin, let it be ever so dirty, for there has, as yet, been no meetings, either for making out Lists, or any other the necessary steps for forming the Militia, and I believe that Prudence will prevent his now taking any measures for putting the late Act in Execution for the Riots it has occasioned in Bedfordshire and other places are enough to deter stouter hearts than his from meddling. I am glad to hear that you and the Gentry you had called together were suffered the other day to go so quietly to ire own homes, for since I heard of poor Sr Rog. Burgoyne's Hair-breadth escape at Biggleswade I shall be apprehensive for every one you shall have for the future. Our Bishop now blesses himself that the Lieutenancy did not fall to his Lot, but I think the less he says of that the better. It is certain that if he had had it, and acted with the same Remissness, the outcry from the Quarter that Power is lodged in would have been grievous, and all charged to the ill Consequences of that being continued in the Hands of an Ecclesiastic.

I thank you much for the News in ire Sect Letter. People have observed our good Bishop look blue (I don't mean true Blue) but they don't know the Cause, for they have not heard of Peggy Bank's Marriage. Some say that she with have had him since he came to the Palatinate, and his Brother's fortune, and that he has refused in his turn. I shall dine with him to morrow, along with Mrs Cowper and Mrs Dolben, and women are such curious observers, that I don't doubt that mine will find out with what kind of Temper he takes Piggy's Match. My Br George writes me word to day that the Fleet was sailed. It is very possible that in some degree the delay might be owing to Domestic Dissensions, but in a much greater, I hear, in having no stores or Ordonance ready to put aboard, and that all was to seek when the Expedition was determined on. If so they have been obliged to the contrary winds for covering their shameful neglect.

I think ire proposal to Amphlett not only kind, but beneficial, if he has stock enough to set out on, but don't know enough of farming or of his affairs to know whether he has sufficient, so can only hope that he will determine on what is best for himself.

I am sorry to find you so low-spirited at the Conclusion of ire first Letter, but hope it was only a transient fit of low spirits which ire Dogs and Pointers have already removed. You'll think me as bad as a chronological Table at the End of an Almanac when I tell you that I remembered Lt Fordwiche's Birth-Day on the 6th.

Ire best Concerts happen generally after I have left Hertfordshire, and I have nothing yet to supply their place, but the little meetings of the Choir-Men at my house, and even they have ceased since Mrs Shirley went. Nine Violins is a strong Reinforcement, and what I shd not have expected at a Hartford Concert. When the Mesh's Geese are put to the Spit, our Concerts begin. I believe one more Winter leaves us Masters of the field, for the Gentlemen-subscribers are heartily sick of the Expense of theirs, and the chief Manager has left this Town and Country for good and all.

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Durham. Dec. 8 1758.

Your Letter, which reached me to day has been of great comfort to me. I could not expect that such a severe stroke wed not have
affected ire health, had you been before right well. I heartily thank God, that you are able to bear up under it at all.

I am much obliged to you for taking on yrself the ordering the Funeral, and am glad that you have concurred in my request that our Sister might be deposited in ire Vault, before you could be acquainted with it. Such a Deviation from her Will is not only pardonable, but I think commendable in such circumstances. The intent of her so ordering it I cannot but imagine was out of a tender regard to us, as I take her sudden removal to Knightsbridge to have been in consequence solely of that intention, when she found her end drawing on. Every other Circumstances of her Will and orders shall be religiously obeyed. I was very much surprised, when I found myself named as Executor, she never having hinted such an intention to me in her Life time. I can only say her Confidence in me shall be repaid by my utmost attention. Mrs. Cowper has wrote by my desire to Williams, and the other serv'ts to remain at board wages till my return. We propose setting out on Monday next, and if nothing obstructs, hope to reach Pansr. by Tuesday se'night. I thank you much my Dear Brother for ire care about my health. I hold out in bodily health tolerably well. Now I may most truly say, Si vales, valeo ; for you are my last stake, poor Mrs Cowper excepted, and I hope you will prize ire health, not only as your own happiness, but as connected with mine too!

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Durham. Dec. 30 1761.
I confess myself ire Debtor for your last, but it is difficult now our Calm is restored to furnish a page out tolerably.

Our Candidates, both the returned and rejected, are gone to try
their fortunes in London. Our friends talk here very sanguinely of their success by Petition, and the other Party (I wish with not more certainty of their Side) say that Lt D. will manage things so as no petition shall be heard this session, and if heard, shall be carried in fav'r of Gowland. It is certain both sides are very active in mustering their Parlt'ry strength, tho the Earl beats us much even in activity. I have wrote to Colleton, but as yet have had no answer. I dare say he's much too Pelhamized to be of any service to us, though my application may prevent his acting against the Gen'l.

I am sorry to hear you have any reason for apprehending a Dropsy. I have still confidence in our AEsculapius of Hatfield, that his Judgment may be taken, and as I remember he considers the swellings of ire Legs as merely Scorbutic. I hope you will stick to ire Horse, whenever the Weather will let you, and for the sake of ire Lungs keep out of that Smoky Town whilst the Fogs and Easterly Winds prevail. I believe the Town is never so unwholesome as when People crowd to it most, in the depth of Winter, when the Smoke hangs over it. I am sure it must in all asthmatic cases, or where the Lungs are weak and apt to be inflamed.

We go on here as to health, as usual. I hope to set out on my Journey by Tuesday next, but hardly shall reach Pans'r till the Wednesday or Thursday following. I intend staying there two or three days after the Brother and Sister are gone to Town, that the fuss of her Visitors may be over before I come, and that I think will bring us there (for I reckon you'll have left the Moat) much about the same Time.
Many happy New Years. We have pretty well travelled through this!

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Pansanger. Feb. 7 1762.

On Friday Morning last Lady Caroline sent for me on some Business. Her Business was when I came, about her Loving and Kind Husband, and introduced by asking me whether I thought you could be induced to see Mr Seymour? I told her, I believed not . She said she hoped you would. That she was now perfectly happy in every other respect . (This she repeated twice with very great Emphasis, leaving me to guess what she meant, and I think I understood it as she was desirous I should) Perfectly happy in every respect , but in regard to the difference between Mr S and you, and she had some hopes that as her happiness was concerned you would be induced to be reconciled to him. What she desired me was to mention her request to you, which I undertook, and told her I would be a faithful messenger, that I wished for every thing that could conduce to her happiness, but that I had little hopes of succeeding in it. Accordingly I went from her directly to your House, but you being gone out, I thought it proper to mention my message to Lie Cowper, who received the Messenger with much greater kindness than his Embassage deserved, and the Message itself with a Temper and coolness peculiar to herself. I will refer myself to her Ladyship for what past, having now discharged my Commission, which I should never have undertaken, had not Lie Car. pressed it upon me in a manner that my Love for her would not let me but feel, and make me inclined to take upon me.

note.value: SPENCER COWPER TO HIS BROTHER WILLIAM COWPER

text.p: Durham. Sept. 1 1764.

Enclosed are the particulars as Lie Gordon gives us them of the application of the Cabbage Leaves. She intends by this Post to inform herself of every other relative to the Progress of the Cure, which I will transmit as soon as I have it. I was mistaken as to the Patient, which was not the D of Perth, who was Lie Gordon's Informant only, but Lie Haggerston of Northumberland, a Catholic Baronet's Lady; but this is not material, as the authority is equaly good. One circumstance of the Cure, you shoud know, for fear it may alarm you, that in Sr Edmd Anderson's case, as well as the Ladies, it raised a temporary Inflammation, in his it was so high as nearly deterred him from pursuing the Medicine, but a Poltice being applied it went down immediately; Lie Haggerston's Legs ran in six days, how long the Cure was working I don't yet know. Lie Gordon mentions nothing of a previous fomentation, nor do I recollect that Circumstance mentioned by Ms Dolben or Lie Milner of the Baronet. I hope you have already data enough to begin on; for I think as Bath Season approaches no time is to be lost. I shall be impatient to know the success, as I unhappily am too far off to watch the progress of it, as I could wish. It cannot have a more quick or perfect Effect than my wishes, and prayers would give it. If it at all
keeps pace with them I shall be excessively happy; and the Credit Sr E. Anderson gives it, who is now seventy two, is sufficient to make me hope the best in your Case, which has by no means those ill Circumstances which his was attended with.
Our Complts to Lie Cowper, Mrs. Cowper's, and Horaces to you.
I forgot to thank you for your first, last Post; when ever you are indisposed to write, the Col. if in the Country, will, as he has promised me, be ire amanuensis.

I dined yesterday at Aukland, and met there Lt Darlington and his Brother. Great good humour and civilities of both sides. On Tuesday I go to Sr Those Clavering's for two or three days, which will be all the Country visits I hope I need make this year. Let gusling at home, and Chapter Squables take up the rest!
